steps.settingDescription: Detective Ira and Chikoo stand inside a grand hall with four locked doors labelled PHRASE, NOUN CLAUSE, RELATIVE CLAUSE, and ADVERBIAL CLAUSE.

dialogues.line: Each door opens only when we identify the exact building block carved on its brass plate!
Easy! Both 'in the dusty attic' and 'because the key was rusty' are groups of words—so both are phrases! Let me push Door 1!

Careful, Chikoo—the door won't budge! 'In the dusty attic' has NO subject and NO finite verb, so it is a Phrase. 'Because the key was rusty' HAS a subject ('the key') and finite verb ('was'), making it a Clause!
And once you spot a subordinate clause, you can tell whether it acts like a Noun, an Adjective (Relative), or an Adverb!

steps.storyCallout: Goal: Distinguish Phrases from Clauses and identify Noun, Adjective/Relative, and Adverbial Clauses.

steps.subtopicTitle: Phrase and Clause Distinction & Phrase Types
steps.memoryAidLabel: Memory Aid (Peculiar Definition — Not a Formal Rule)
steps.peculiarDefinition: A Phrase is a team of words WITHOUT a Subject–Finite-Verb heartbeat; a Clause is a mini-sentence WITH its own Subject + Finite Verb engine.
steps.formalDefinition: A phrase is a grammatically related group of words that lacks a subject–finite-verb pair and functions as a single part of speech (noun, adjective, adverb, or prepositional unit). A clause is a group of words containing a subject and a finite verb.
steps.simpleExplanation: Always check for a finite verb with a subject! 'At the crack of dawn' = Phrase (no finite verb). 'When the sun rose' = Clause ('the sun' + finite verb 'rose'). Phrases act as noun phrases ('a stack of old letters'), adjective phrases ('full of clues'), or adverb phrases ('with great care').

structurePatterns.formula: Acts as Subject, Object, or Complement
structurePatterns.sample: [The brass compass on the desk] points north.
The boy [wearing a yellow kurta] solved the riddle.
Detective Ira inspected the lock [with extreme care].

realLifeExamples.sentence: To solve this mystery quickly is our top priority.
realLifeExamples.contextNote: 'To solve this mystery quickly' is an infinitive Noun Phrase acting as Subject (no finite verb inside it).

realLifeExamples.sentence: We waited until the rain stopped.
realLifeExamples.contextNote: 'until the rain stopped' is an Adverb Clause because 'the rain' (subject) + 'stopped' (finite verb) appear inside it.

correctVsIncorrect.incorrectSentence: Calling 'before sunset' a clause because it has 'before'.
correctVsIncorrect.correctSentence: 'before sunset' = Prepositional Phrase; 'before the sun set' = Clause.
correctVsIncorrect.whyItHappens: Words like 'before', 'after', and 'until' act as prepositions before a noun phrase ('before sunset') and as subordinators before a subject + finite verb ('before the sun set').

exceptions: Participial ('running fast') and infinitive ('to win the race') groups are non-finite phrases, not finite clauses.

steps.storyPrompt: Door 1 displays four inscriptions. Only ONE is a CLAUSE (containing a subject and finite verb).
steps.questionPrompt: Select the inscription that is a CLAUSE:
options: while the grandfather clock struck twelve
acceptedAnswers: while the grandfather clock struck twelve
steps.hint: Look for a subject doing a tensed action (a finite verb) inside the group of words.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Detective Ira: "Click! Door 1 swings open! 'the grandfather clock' is the subject and 'struck' is the finite verb."
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Check whether the group has a real Subject + Finite Verb pair. Prepositions, 'to'-infinitives, and '-ed' participles alone form phrases.

feedbackWrongByOption.covered in thick silver dust: Participial phrase—lacks a subject and finite auxiliary.

steps.simplerExample: 'after dinner' = Phrase | 'after we ate dinner' = Clause.

steps.subtopicTitle: Noun Clauses, Adjective/Relative Clauses & Adverbial Clauses
steps.memoryAidLabel: Memory Aid (Peculiar Definition — Not a Formal Rule)
steps.peculiarDefinition: Subordinate clauses are master disguisers: a Noun Clause wears a 'WHAT/THAT' badge and sits in a noun's chair; a Relative Clause clings right behind a noun like a sticky bio-tag ('who/which/that'); an Adverbial Clause tells the verb WHEN, WHERE, WHY, or IF.
steps.formalDefinition: Subordinate (dependent) clauses perform three major grammatical functions: Noun Clauses replace noun phrases (as subject, object, complement, or object of preposition); Adjective/Relative Clauses post-modify a noun/pronoun; Adverbial Clauses modify a verb, adjective, or main clause (expressing time, place, reason, condition, purpose, result, or concession).
steps.simpleExplanation: Use quick replacement tests! (1) Replace the clause with 'SOMETHING / IT': if the sentence stays grammatical ('I know SOMETHING' ← 'I know [that Ira is right]'), it is a NOUN clause! (2) Check if it follows and describes a noun ('the detective [who found the clue]'): RELATIVE/ADJECTIVE clause! (3) Check if it answers 'when/why/where/under what condition': ADVERBIAL clause!

structurePatterns.formula: that / what / whether / if / wh-word + S + V
structurePatterns.sample: [What Chikoo said] surprised everyone. / We wondered [whether the gate was locked].

structurePatterns.formula: Noun + who / whom / whose / which / that + Clause
structurePatterns.sample: The key [that opened the chest] was hidden inside a book.

structurePatterns.formula: when, while, because, since, if, unless, although, so that + S + V

realLifeExamples.sentence: Tell me where you found the brass seal.
realLifeExamples.contextNote: Noun Clause as Direct Object ('Tell me SOMETHING'). Notice statement word order ('you found', NOT 'did you find').

realLifeExamples.sentence: The student whose essay won the medal lives in Shillong.

correctVsIncorrect.incorrectSentence: I don't know where did Chikoo hide the bananas.
correctVsIncorrect.correctSentence: I don't know where Chikoo hid the bananas.
correctVsIncorrect.whyItHappens: Inside a Noun Clause embedded within a statement, use normal Subject + Verb order ('Chikoo hid'), NOT question inversion ('did Chikoo hide').

exceptions: Don't confuse Noun vs. Relative clauses both starting with 'where' or 'who': 'I know [where he lives]' (Noun Clause, no antecedent noun) vs. 'I visited the village [where he lives]' (Relative Clause modifying 'the village').

steps.subtopicTitle: Noun vs. Relative vs. Adverbial Clause
steps.storyPrompt: Door 2 shows a riddle: "Detective Ira examined the map [that lay on the table]."
steps.questionPrompt: What type of subordinate clause is "that lay on the table"?
steps.hint: Look right before 'that lay on the table'—which noun is it describing?
steps.feedbackCorrect: Vaani: "Door 2 unlocks! It sits immediately after the noun 'map' and tells us WHICH map, so it is an Adjective/Relative Clause."
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Notice two clues: it has a finite verb ('lay'), and it describes the noun 'the map'.

feedbackWrongByOption.Noun Clause: Try replacing it with 'something': 'Detective Ira examined the map SOMETHING' makes no sense!
feedbackWrongByOption.Adverbial Clause of Place: It doesn't tell where Ira examined; it describes WHICH map.

steps.simplerExample: The book [that I borrowed] is exciting. (Describes 'book' = Relative Clause).

steps.stepTitle: Checkpoint 3: Fix Chikoo's Embedded Noun Clause
steps.storyPrompt: Chikoo whispers to the guard: "Please tell me what time does the puzzle house close."
steps.questionPrompt: Choose the grammatically accurate Noun Clause version:
options: Please tell me what time does the puzzle house closes.
Please tell me what time the puzzle house closes.
Please tell me what time is closing the puzzle house.
Please tell me does what time the puzzle house close.
acceptedAnswers: Please tell me what time the puzzle house closes.
steps.hint: Inside an embedded Noun Clause, drop the question auxiliary 'does' and put Subject + Verb in statement order.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Acharya Vidyadhar: "Door 3 opens! Inside a Noun Clause object, keep Subject ('the puzzle house') before Verb ('closes')."
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Remove 'does' and place the subject before the verb: 'what time the puzzle house closes'.
steps.simplerExample: Do you know where Rohan lives? (NOT: where does Rohan live?)

steps.stepTitle: Checkpoint 4: Unlock the Final Clause Door
steps.storyPrompt: Door 4 shows a conditional clue: "You cannot open the treasure box ______ you find the matching relative pronoun."
steps.questionPrompt: Type the single best subordinating conjunction meaning 'if not' (one word):
steps.sentenceTemplate: You cannot open the treasure box ______ you find the matching relative pronoun.
steps.hint: Which 6-letter conjunction means 'if you do not'?
steps.feedbackCorrect: Detective Ira: "Door 4 clicks open! 'Unless' introduces a negative conditional Adverbial Clause ('if you do not find...')."
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Think of the single subordinating conjunction that replaces 'if ... not' without adding 'not' again.

feedbackWrongByOption.until: Close in context, though 'unless' specifically means 'if not' as a condition.

steps.simplerExample: You will miss the train unless you hurry.

steps.settingDescription: All four brass doors stand wide open, revealing the golden crest of The Sentence Kingdom.

dialogues.line: Every phrase and clause clicked neatly into place—no fragment or mislabelled clause can fool us now.
I know [that we make a great team] (Noun Clause!) because [we solved every clue together] (Adverbial Clause!)!

steps.storyCallout: Module 4 Story Complete! Check your Grammar Notebook and conquer the World 1 Final Assessment.

summaryRules.heading: Phrase vs. Clause
summaryRules.ruleSummary: A Phrase is a related word group WITHOUT a Subject + Finite Verb pair. A Clause contains a Subject + Finite Verb.
summaryRules.formulaOrPattern: Phrase (no finite verb) vs. Clause (Subject + Finite Verb)
summaryRules.example: Phrase: 'during the storm' | Clause: 'while the storm raged'

summaryRules.heading: Noun Clause
summaryRules.ruleSummary: Acts as a noun (Subject, Direct Object, Complement, or Object of Preposition); passes the 'SOMETHING / IT' replacement test.
summaryRules.formulaOrPattern: that / what / whether / if / wh-word + Subject + Verb

summaryRules.heading: Adjective (Relative) Clause
summaryRules.ruleSummary: Follows and describes a noun/pronoun (the antecedent), introduced by who, whom, whose, which, that, where, or when.
summaryRules.example: The notebook [that I lost] turned up in the lab.

summaryRules.heading: Adverbial Clause
summaryRules.ruleSummary: Modifies a verb, adjective, or main clause to express time, place, reason, condition, purpose, comparison, or concession.
summaryRules.formulaOrPattern: when, while, because, since, if, unless, although, so that + S + V
summaryRules.example: Although the trail was steep, we reached the top.

memoryAids: Phrase = no heartbeat (no finite verb); Clause = has a Subject + Finite Verb engine.
Noun Clause = 'SOMETHING' replacement test; Relative Clause = sticky bio-tag behind a noun; Adverbial Clause = answers when/why/where/if.

commonMistakes.incorrectSentence: Tell me where did you keep the key.
commonMistakes.correctSentence: Tell me where you kept the key.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Embedded Noun Clauses use statement word order (Subject before Verb), never question 'do/did' inversion.

commonMistakes.incorrectSentence: Unless you do not work hard, you will fail.
commonMistakes.correctSentence: Unless you work hard, you will fail.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: 'Unless' already means 'if not', so adding 'not' creates an illogical double negative.

exceptions: Relative clauses with 'where/when' always follow a noun ('the day when we met'), whereas Noun clauses with 'where/when' stand in for a noun slot ('I remember when we met').
textbookNotes: Consolidated coverage of Phrases, Main/Subordinate Clauses, Noun, Relative, and Adverbial Clauses.

questions.questionText: Which group of words is a PHRASE (not a clause)?
questions.explanation: 'across the crowded courtyard' has no subject and no finite verb, so it is a prepositional phrase.
distractorRationales: Correct: preposition + noun phrase, zero finite verb.
questions.grammarRule: A phrase contains no subject–finite-verb pair.

questions.questionText: In "The athlete ran with remarkable speed", what type of phrase is "with remarkable speed"?
questions.explanation: It modifies the verb 'ran' by telling HOW the athlete ran (= remarkably fast), functioning as an Adverb phrase.
distractorRationales: Does not occupy a noun slot.
questions.grammarRule: A prepositional phrase modifying a verb functions as an Adverb phrase.

questions.questionText: Identify the clause type of "[that the parcel arrived safely]" in "We are glad [that the parcel arrived safely]."
questions.explanation: A 'that'-clause completing an adjective ('glad') or verb ('know/think') functions as a Noun clause (nominal complement).
distractorRationales: There is no noun antecedent for 'that' to describe.
questions.grammarRule: 'That'-clauses serving as subject, object, or adjective/verb complement are Noun clauses.

questions.questionText: In "The bridge [which crosses the Brahmaputra] is illuminated at night", what is "which crosses the Brahmaputra"?
questions.explanation: It follows and defines the noun 'The bridge', acting as an Adjective/Relative clause.
distractorRationales: Does not modify the verb 'is illuminated'.
Contains finite verb 'crosses', so it is a clause.
questions.grammarRule: A clause introduced by who/which/that modifying an antecedent noun is an Adjective/Relative clause.

questions.questionText: In "Stay under the shelter until the hailstorm stops", what kind of clause is "until the hailstorm stops"?
questions.explanation: 'until the hailstorm stops' has subject + finite verb and tells WHEN/HOW LONG to stay.
distractorRationales: Does not occupy a noun position.
questions.grammarRule: Clauses introduced by when, while, before, after, until, since (time) are Adverbial clauses of time.

questions.questionText: In "[Whoever finishes first] will ring the brass bell", what role does the bracketed clause play?
questions.explanation: 'Whoever finishes first' occupies the Subject slot right before the main verb 'will ring' (Test: 'HE/SOMEONE will ring...').
distractorRationales: Correct: Noun clause in Subject position.
It sits before the main verb, not after 'bell'.
questions.grammarRule: A Noun clause can serve directly as the Subject of a main verb.

options: Can you explain why did the experiment fail?
Can you explain why the experiment failed?
Can you explain why failed the experiment?
Can you explain did why the experiment fail?
questions.explanation: 'Can you explain' already performs the question inversion; the embedded Noun clause keeps normal order: 'why the experiment failed'.
distractorRationales: Double inversion ('did ... fail') inside embedded clause.
questions.grammarRule: Embedded wh-noun clauses use statement word order, not question inversion.

questions.questionText: Fix the error in: "You won't catch the morning bus unless you do not leave now."
options: You won't catch the morning bus unless you leave now.
You won't catch the morning bus if you leave now.
You won't catch the morning bus unless you won't leave now.
questions.explanation: 'Unless' already means 'if ... not', so adding 'do not' reverses the meaning into a double negative.
distractorRationales: Uses 'will' inside conditional clause plus double negative.
questions.grammarRule: Use an affirmative verb after 'unless' (= 'if not').

questions.questionText: In which sentence is "where the river bends" a RELATIVE (Adjective) clause?
options: Nobody knows where the river bends.
Where the river bends is a calm spot for herons.
We camped at the meadow where the river bends.
Ask the guide where the river bends.
questions.explanation: In option C, 'where the river bends' directly follows and modifies the noun 'the meadow', making it a Relative clause.
questions.grammarRule: A 'where/when' clause modifying a preceding noun is Relative; without an antecedent noun, it is usually a Noun or Adverbial clause.

questions.questionText: Compare (1) "before the final whistle" and (2) "before the referee blew the whistle". Which statement is accurate?
options: (1) is a phrase and (2) is a clause.
(1) is a clause and (2) is a phrase.
questions.explanation: (1) has only a noun phrase after 'before' (no finite verb), whereas (2) has subject 'the referee' + finite verb 'blew'.
questions.grammarRule: Preposition + NP = Phrase; Subordinator + S + Finite Verb = Clause.

questions.subtopicTitle: Relative pronouns who vs whom vs whose
questions.questionText: Choose the right relative word: "The artist ______ painting won the state award is my aunt."
questions.explanation: 'Whose' shows possession linking 'The artist' to 'painting' ('the artist's painting').
distractorRationales: 'Whom' is an object pronoun, not possessive.
questions.grammarRule: Use 'whose' in relative clauses to show possession.

questions.questionText: Which conjunction introduces an Adverbial Clause of CONCESSION (unexpected contrast)?
questions.explanation: 'Although / though / even though' introduces a fact that contrasts surprisingly with the main clause (concession).
questions.grammarRule: Concessive adverbial clauses use although, though, even though, or even if.

questions.questionText: In "The mango tree laden with ripe fruit shaded the bench", what is "laden with ripe fruit"?
questions.explanation: 'Laden with ripe fruit' has no finite verb (it's a participial/adjective phrase) and describes 'The mango tree'.
distractorRationales: No finite verb, so not a clause.
Not a noun slot and no finite verb.
questions.grammarRule: An adjective/participial phrase following a noun modifies that noun without adding a finite clause.

questions.questionText: Identify the function of the Noun Clause in "Everything depends on [whether the monsoon arrives on time]."
questions.explanation: It follows the preposition 'on' and passes the replacement test: 'Everything depends on THAT/IT'.
distractorRationales: Correct: Noun clause serving as object of preposition 'on'.
Does not describe 'Everything' as a relative clause.
questions.grammarRule: A Noun clause can serve as the object of a preposition.

questions.questionText: Complete the sentence with an Adverbial Clause of PURPOSE: "Detective Ira carried a torch ______."
options: so that she could inspect the dark cellar
questions.explanation: 'so that she could inspect the dark cellar' explains the intended purpose/goal of carrying the torch.
distractorRationales: Adverbial clause of reason, not purpose.
questions.grammarRule: Adverbial clauses of purpose commonly use 'so that / in order that + subject + can/could/may/might'.
